extracted.intended_audience: researchers, practitioners, and prospective authors/attendees in human–computer interaction considering CHI
extracted.subtask_description: Determine whether a research or practice contribution fits CHI (the ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems) by considering its track, topical scope, competitiveness, and community impact. Useful for prospective submitters and reviewers to gauge expectations and fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference prestige / standing
rubrics_metrics.description: The ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI) series of academic conferences is generally considered the most prestigious in the field of human–computer interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige implies high expectations for novelty, rigor, and impact; authors should target high-quality work and reviewers should expect leading-edge contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity / acceptance rate
rubrics_metrics.description: After the early years CHI became highly selective. Since 1993 the acceptance rate for full papers was consistently below 30 percent. After 1992 the average acceptance rate was around 20 percent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the low acceptance rate as an indication of competitiveness: submissions must be strong on originality, methodological rigor, and significance to have a good chance of acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of accepted full papers
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of accepted full papers is slowly increasing and reached 157 accepted papers with an acceptance rate of 22 percent in 2008.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both absolute accepted-paper counts and acceptance percentages are useful metrics for understanding program size and selectivity in a given year; authors can infer how many slots are typically available for full papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission tracks — Academic papers and notes (short papers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic papers and notes (short papers) on a variety of topics, such as ubiquitous computing, visualization, usability and user experience design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full papers are for complete research contributions; notes/short papers are for more focused or preliminary contributions. Ensure topical fit (HCI-related areas) and conform to the specific track's length and content expectations (see CHI call for papers for exact limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission tracks — Posters and demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posters/demos are the appropriate format for work-in-progress, prototypes, or interactive systems that benefit from hands-on or visual presentation rather than a full paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission tracks — Workshops and courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops and courses hosted by domain experts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshops/courses are for community building, in-depth tutorials, or focused discussions led by experts; proposals should justify community need and include plans for participation and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission tracks — Invited panels
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels are for curated discussions of timely or controversial topics; panels are typically organized by conveners and invitees and should offer diverse perspectives and clear discussion goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission tracks — Case studies from industry practitioners
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry case studies are a recognized track for practice-oriented contributions; they should present real-world problems, approaches taken, and reflective lessons or evidence of impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical scope (HCI subject areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Topics such as ubiquitous computing, visualization, usability and user experience design (and broadly, human–computer interaction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions should align with HCI topics listed; topical fit is a primary filter at submission and review stages. Authors should emphasize relevance to HCI audiences and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference size / attendance as community impact metric
rubrics_metrics.description: CHI attracts thousands of international attendees (examples: CHI reached over 3,300 attendees in 2013; 3,855 in 2019; 5,145 in 2021 virtual; 4,721 in 2023).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large attendance indicates visibility and community reach—authors seeking wide dissemination should value CHI's audience; reviewers and program chairs may consider potential community impact when selecting contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational sponsorship and publication venue
rubrics_metrics.description: CHI is hosted by ACM SIGCHI, and associated with ACM (publisher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsorship by ACM/SIGCHI implies formal proceedings and archival publication practices (e.g., ACM Digital Library). Submissions must meet ACM's formatting and ethical/policy requirements (check CHI/ACM submission guidelines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Event timing and frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Since its start CHI conferences have been held annually in spring each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and organizers should plan around the annual submission/review cycle; recurrent scheduling affects project timelines and readiness of work for submission.
